Dog runs on Conway's lakefront and inland lots alike

A dog run on the Lake Conway chain has to answer to the state's 10-foot waterbody setback before anything else; one three blocks inland usually doesn't. Pet turf here runs $10–$18 per square foot as of September 2026, drains fast enough for daily rinsing, and skips the weed barrier a plain lawn often gets.

Reviewed by Luis Austin, owner · Last reviewed September 21, 2026

Say you have a 240 sq ft dog run along a lakefront fence line

A 240 square foot run along a Conway lakefront fence, common on an older lot where the dog yard sits between the house and the seawall, prices between $2,880 and $3,840 at the published $12–$16 typical range. If that fence line sits within ten feet of the water and there's no seawall to claim the exception, the buildable run shrinks and the price follows the smaller footprint rather than the fence's actual length. On an inland Conway lot with no waterbody nearby, the same 240 square feet turfs at the identical rate, since the price range itself never changes; only the buildable area does.

Where a fenced yard meets 1,771 acres of connected lake

The Conway chain, Lake Conway and the smaller waters tied to it by canal, covers 1,771 surface acres according to the county's own water atlas (the Lake Conway entry), and a dog run on that shoreline sits inside the state's 10-foot setback zone unless a seawall or bulkhead already separates the yard from the water. Older Conway seawalls, some dating to the same 1950s and 60s wave of construction as the homes behind them, usually qualify for that exception, but a dock or a rock revetment alone does not. Staking the actual buildable line before ordering material keeps a dog-run quote honest about how much of a waterfront yard the rule allows to be turfed.

Keeping odor-control infill from washing toward the drain

The state's rule that infill must not wash off the property applies to a Conway dog run's zeolite or coated sand exactly as it does to a plain lawn's silica, and a run graded toward one drain point concentrates rinse water enough that a lighter infill grain can travel further than it would across an open lawn's gentler runoff. Choosing a slightly heavier grain of whichever infill a run uses, and keeping the drain-point grade no steeper than it needs to be, keeps the odor-control material where it's actually doing its job instead of collecting at the low point.

Grading a run toward Boggy Creek's own drainage, not away from it

Conway's chain drains south into the Boggy Creek Watershed, whose namesake stream feeds East Lake Tohopekaliga and puts the community under the South Florida Water Management District's Kissimmee Basin planning area rather than the St. Johns district that covers most of Orange County (Boggy Creek Watershed, general information). A dog run's own grading has nothing to do with that district line directly, but it matters for the irrigation question: whichever utility bills a specific Conway address, Orange County Utilities or OUC, its schedule stops applying to synthetic turf the moment the zone's heads are capped, which the state standard already requires.

Grading a dog run toward a drain, not just away from the house

A plain lawn only needs its subgrade sloped away from the foundation, but a Conway dog run gets graded toward a specific low point or drain instead, since rinse water and urine both need somewhere consistent to go rather than just somewhere away from the house. That drain point is also chosen to keep liquid moving away from a patio slab or pool deck edge, since concrete holds odor differently than turf does and a slab that stays damp near a dog area tends to stain over time. The one to two percent grade itself doesn't change, only the direction it's aimed and the reason behind picking that direction.

When odor infill leaves the yard during a storm

The state's rule against infill washing off the property applies to a Conway dog run's zeolite or coated sand as much as it does to any lawn's silica, and a run graded too steeply toward its drain point can carry a visible amount of infill past the property line during a hard rain, sometimes into a neighbor's yard downhill. That's a different failure than the run simply smelling because of a shallow base; it's a drainage and grading problem showing up as material loss rather than odor. A gentler grade at the drain point and a properly finished edge there keep infill from becoming the storm's collateral damage.

Capping irrigation as part of a pet-yard build

Any sprinkler zone crossing a Conway dog run's footprint gets capped at the valve box during the base-building phase, the same step a lawn conversion goes through, since the state's rule against watering synthetic turf with an in-ground system applies to a pet area exactly the way it applies anywhere else on the lot. From that point forward, a hose handles both rinsing and any supplemental water the yard needs. This step happens early enough in the process that a crew isn't reopening finished rock work later to reach a buried line near the run.

Clearing waste and debris so the base keeps draining

Solid waste left sitting on a Conway dog run works down into the infill layer over time rather than staying on the surface, and once it's mixed in there, the same washed-rock base built to move liquid through quickly ends up working harder to do that job. Picking it up on a routine that doesn't lag more than a day or two, especially during the busiest summer stretch, keeps the base's percolation doing what it's designed for instead of fighting through material it was never meant to filter. This is one habit that matters more on a dedicated run than almost anywhere else on the property.

Odor control on an older ranch lot's fenced side yard

Conway's ranch homes typically carry a fenced side or back yard sized for a family dog rather than a purpose-built kennel run, and on an 8,000 to 12,000 square foot lot that fenced area is usually a modest slice of the total (a Conway lot-size profile). Zeolite or coated-sand infill fits that scale well, since a smaller area means rinsing takes less water and less time even on a hot Conway afternoon, and neither infill choice conflicts with the state's natural-material rule the way rubber crumb would.

Our piece on clearing dog urine odor from turf covers the rinsing routine behind that infill choice, and the pet turf and dog run guide goes through backing and drainage specs in more depth. The Conway turf guide above has the lake chain's setback figures; Belle Isle, Orlando and Edgewood all border the same water system from a different side.

Questions people ask

Does an older Conway seawall automatically qualify for the setback exception?

Usually, if it's an intact seawall or bulkhead separating the yard from the water. A dock, a wood bulkhead in poor repair, or a rock revetment alone doesn't automatically qualify, so it's worth pointing the seawall out to the crew during the site visit rather than assuming.

Which water utility do I check before scheduling irrigation capping in Conway?

Look at a recent bill. Orange County Utilities serves most of the unincorporated community, and the Orlando Utilities Commission bills some addresses closer to the city line, but the capping step and its timing in the build don't change based on which one appears on the bill.
